fetched_contents.text: Similarity-based Multi-Domain Dialogue State Tracking with Copy Mechanisms for Task-based Virtual Personal Assistants Abstract Abstract Task-based Virtual Personal Assistants (VPAs) rely on multi-domain Dialogue State Tracking (DST) models to monitor goals throughout a conversation. Previously proposed models show promising results on established benchmarks, but they have difficulty adapting to unseen domains due to domain-specific parameters in their model architectures. We propose a new Similarity-based Multi-domain Dialogue State Tracking model (SM-DST) that uses retrieval-inspired and fine-grained contextual token-level similarity approaches to efficiently and effectively track dialogue state. The key difference with state-of-the-art DST models is that SM-DST has a single model with shared parameters across domains and slots. Because we base SM-DST on similarity it allows the transfer of tracking information between semantically related domains as well as to unseen domains without retraining. Furthermore, we leverage copy mechanisms that consider the system’s response and the dialogue state from previous turn predictions, allowing it to more effectively track dialogue state for complex conversations. We evaluate SM-DST on three variants of the MultiWOZ DST benchmark datasets. The results demonstrate that SM-DST significantly and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models across all datasets by absolute 5-18% and 3-25% in the few- and zero-shot settings, respectively. The evidence does not directly say how TRADE explicitly addresses all these limitations, but it does indicate that the model’s design helps mitigate them. The DST paper’s parameter sharing and transfer mechanism reduce the need for full retraining per domain [N1-F1]. The benchmark evidence also suggests that cross-domain methods can achieve significant gains, especially in few- and zero-shot settings, which implies that the model can still be useful when labeled target data is sparse [N3-F2]. Still, the limitations remain: domain shift can occur, data annotation may be incomplete or expensive, and practical deployment may require adaptation under turn-level supervision or other constraints [N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R1].

### 4) Bottom line: how TRADE enables effective knowledge transfer

Overall, the evidence supports the idea that TRADE-like methods enable effective knowledge transfer in dialogue state tracking by combining a multi-domain DST architecture with transfer learning. The core components are slot-value independence, parameter sharing, candidate generation, and reuse of learned representations across domains [N1-F1]. This makes the model easier to adapt to new domains than standard DST, which often requires separate training for each domain [N1-F1].

The model’s transfer effectiveness is strongest when the new domain is semantically related and when the model can use retrieval-inspired similarity or copy mechanisms to maintain state consistency over turns [N3-F2]. The benchmark evidence shows that such methods can outperform state-of-the-art DST models in few- and zero-shot settings, which is a strong indicator that transfer is useful in practical DST settings [N3-F2].

At the same time, the evidence also shows that domain transfer is not guaranteed. Transfer can fail when the source and target domains differ substantially, when labeled data is insufficient, or when evaluation constraints do not reflect real-world deployment conditions [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-R1]. So, while TRADE-like methods make knowledge transfer more feasible, they do not eliminate the risks of domain mismatch, data scarcity, and deployment constraints [N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R1].

## Conclusion

In short, the TRADE model enables effective knowledge transfer across domains in dialogue state tracking by using a multi-domain DST architecture that shares parameters across slots and domains, and by transferring learned representations rather than retraining from scratch [N1-F1]. It is particularly effective when the model can also use similarity-based adaptation, copy mechanisms, or other cross-domain strategies to maintain state consistency across turns [N3-F2]. However, its effectiveness depends on alignment between source and target domains, availability of labeled data, and the realism of the evaluation setup [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-R1].
